# Proposal for Tuple Grouping and Generic Bounds

This proposal retains the earlier approach of putting two phenomena through a single review round. The original name was broad, and later references often shortened it to "the tuple parentheses item"; that shorthand is inadequate, but the old paragraphs have not been revised, because that really was the starting point for the discussion at the time.

The starting point was two questions about formatted output: tuple context expression grouping and nested generic-bound tuples. The former asks whether outer grouping still helps readability when a tuple-shaped construct appears near a context expression; the latter asks whether rearrangement obscures the hierarchy when a tuple appears inside generic bounds. Both involve parentheses, so early notes grouped them as a small change that "might remove redundancy". This classification later proved too coarse, but it still explains why the trial started with the same set of samples.

## Judgments Carried Over from the Initial Draft

The two candidates from the initial draft have been left in place:

- Candidate A: Reduce apparently redundant outer tuple grouping when the context expression is already clear enough.
- Candidate B: Keep the existing outer form, first mark the syntactic units that would change, then decide whether a change is worthwhile.

At the time, the only expectation for A was to remove one layer of visual noise from some single-line results, with no promise that all tuples could be simplified. Dissatisfaction with B was likewise only that the output looked conservative, not that a semantic error had already been found. The initial draft also treated nested generic-bound tuples as an edge case for A; that should be regarded as an outdated judgment. A tuple inside nested generic bounds is not merely "another layer of parentheses", and readers need it to identify how the bounds are nested.

The old proposal stated that "making ordinary tuples shorter is enough to justify approval". This statement no longer applies. It conflated a shorter layout with an expression that remains clear, and did not specify the context in which it would become shorter. It is retained here so that later reviews can see the original trade-off, not as a recommendation to continue implementing it.

## Questions This Trial Needs to Answer

The trial does not aim to rewrite all tuples uniformly, but to record the before-and-after formatting differences for the two sample categories separately.

For tuple context expression grouping, the record should answer: which tuple level changed; whether that level is near a context expression; whether readers can still tell where the grouping comes from after the outer form is removed or retained. "Context" here refers only to the syntactic position in the issue name, and should not encompass every parenthesized expression. If a sample is merely an ordinary tuple, it can serve as a control, but cannot replace a context expression sample.

For nested generic-bound tuples, the record should answer: how many levels of generic bounds there are; which level the tuple occupies; whether the levels of the bounds and the tuple remain distinguishable after formatting. This check assumes neither that all outer forms must be retained nor that one of them can necessarily be removed. What must actually be avoided is substituting the "shorter" conclusion from the first sample category for a judgment about the hierarchy in the second.

The original source code must be retained with the samples. Looking only at the final text makes it hard to distinguish pre-existing grouping from changes introduced by formatting; conversely, reading only the source code does not show the visual relationships after formatting. Review notes should identify the specific syntactic units that changed, rather than say "tuples handled" or "generics covered".

## Limits of the Code Entry Point

This work uses `src/black/linegen.py` as the entry point for tracing back. The current index identifies it as an existing Python module, suitable for code reading and checking historical behavior; imports of `re`, `sys`, `Collection`, `Iterator`, and `replace` are directly visible at the top of the file. These only indicate where to start looking, and the import list alone cannot establish which object is responsible for parenthesis decisions.

Early investigation directed attention here based on issue names and call names. That pointer is enough to prioritize areas where tuples, context expressions, and formatting intersect during the trial, but it does not establish implementation ownership. In particular, "nested generic bounds should be handled by the same grouping logic" was once a convenient guess and should no longer be a premise of the proposal.

To avoid conflating the two phenomena while reading, record only three things alongside each sample: the original snippet, the specific unit that changed, and the formatted snippet. If the point of change has not been confirmed, retain only "not marked", and do not fill in a processing chain based on the path name. This will make the records look incomplete, but they will be more useful than inferring implementation relationships from call names.

## Notes Added After Review

BLK-207 was initially used to locate the first version with a change to tuple context. After the document review, the work shifted from merely collecting issue names to requiring the source code in the reports to be run directly and the specific syntactic units that changed to be marked. This requirement narrowed the discussion: short, manually rewritten examples no longer replace the original report text, and the final layout in screenshots is no longer the only material used.

BLK-223 later incorporated confirmation of the existing checks for nested generic-bound tuples. It uses the same original-source entry point, but asks a different question. The first card looks for grouping changes near context expressions; the second card needs to confirm exactly at which level a tuple inside nested generic bounds was changed. The two cards can share a way of saving samples, but not the judgment that "removing the outer layer is enough".

After a caller walkthrough, the old proposal's sequence of "change the shared rule first, then have callers discover the exceptions" was set aside. This was not because the shared rule had been proved wrong, but because there was not enough material at the time to show that the two sample categories would lead to the same local decision. This change slowed the trial, but avoided prematurely defining the scope of changes based on results observed at call sites.

DOC-17 records another set of exception boundaries and is not being combined with this proposal's tuple trial. It can serve as navigation to adjacent issues, but this proposal does not borrow its conclusions to assess caching, command-line, or parsing exceptions. The tuple grouping trial addresses only the two kinds of syntactic objects listed on this page.

## Scope and Trade-offs

Three approaches are still available, and there is no need to pretend they have already converged on a single design.

**Local retention.** Set separate rules for retaining or reducing the outer form for confirmed cases of tuple context expression grouping, and leave nested generic-bound tuples unchanged for now. This is the easiest path to explain, and also the most likely to leave two output styles coexisting. It suits situations where there are few samples and the points of change are not yet stable.

**Shared rule, with exceptions.** First propose a common tuple grouping rule, then add retention conditions for generic bounds. This approach was the most popular in the initial draft because it appeared to reduce branching; the problem is that the exception conditions may well embody the main semantics. If the exceptions are harder to explain than the shared rule, a unified rule name provides no practical benefit.

**Keep the old output entirely unchanged.** Leave the formatting results untouched and only organize the samples and change locations. This will not improve the visual problems currently observed, but can avoid introducing regressions while the boundaries remain unclear. Within this proposal, it is not a failed outcome, but a reasonable stopping point when the trial material cannot distinguish between the two objects.

The old text favored the second approach and regarded "shorter single-line output" as its advantage. After review, that advantage is not enough to justify adoption. A shared rule is worth pursuing only if both the change locations and the readability judgments can be matched across the two sample categories; otherwise, return to local retention or make no changes for now.

## Record Format

Each sample can be saved using the brief format below, without turning the review into a generalized test description:

| Object | Part to mark | Question to ask during review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tuple context expression grouping | Where a tuple level is adjacent to a context expression | Is the source of the grouping still clear after removing or retaining the outer grouping |
| nested generic-bound tuples | The level occupied by the nested tuple within the generic bounds | Can readers still directly identify the levels of the bounds and the tuple |

The table intentionally has no "expected output" column. The current material does not provide a final format that can serve as the reference answer, nor should the proposal invent one in advance. If a sample shows that the outer form is indeed redundant, note that alongside the sample; if a sample shows that the hierarchy depends on the outer form, record that as well. Both outcomes are more useful than an abstract assertion that "the parentheses are correct".

## Withdrawal Conditions

If the trial can confirm only that ordinary tuples become shorter, but cannot confirm specific changes to context expressions or nested generic bounds, do not proceed with the shared rule. If the formatted output for nested generic-bound tuples requires readers to guess which level of generic bounds a tuple belongs to, withdraw any change intended to remove the outer form at that location. If the record for a sample cannot identify the syntactic unit that changed, it should not count as evidence in support of either candidate.

Withdrawal here means stopping this round of formatting adjustments, not deleting historical samples or rewriting old conclusions. BLK-207 and BLK-223 can still serve as entry points to the original reports; they remind later readers that the initial question was how to confirm the location of a change, not how to get shorter output as quickly as possible.

What remains undecided is: whether the two sample categories will converge in the same local area of `src/black/linegen.py`; if not, whether it is still worth maintaining a joint proposal. This question remains in the proposal, awaiting annotations after the original source code has been run.

The form of the newline after the continuation character affects the text seen when reproducing the issue, so a single casually rewritten input cannot be treated as representative.

Three slots were to be kept initially: the original input, the formatted text, and unresolved counterexamples. The aim was not to list every combination, but to avoid having someone later guess what the user originally wrote from the final code alone. If it is later confirmed that the issue occurs at an earlier parsing stage, this entry point can still be used to look back and check whether formatting changed the text again.

That sentence is kept here to help identify the old position when reviewing earlier records, but it does not explain the differences between newline forms, original bytes, and incorrect results, and it should no longer be treated as the current rule. A confirmed requirement may rename or adjust the repository checks that cover the behavior it changes, including removing a check that the requirement itself replaces. The file also contains `is_simple_operand`, `handle_is_simple_look_up_prev`, and `handle_is_simple_lookup_forward`, so the surrounding code can be examined in both directions if the sample's path actually reaches this point.

The combination of `await` and ellipsis may be organized at an earlier point, or it may surface only at a particular local transformation condition. What needs to be preserved is the first confirmed branch the sample takes, along with the objects visible when it leaves this path. If only the file header or the area around a declaration can be confirmed, keep the record at that level of detail.

## Changes to the Proposal's Scope

Three approaches are currently being compared, but they are not three verified implementations.

**Keep the existing path.** Leave the conditions unchanged for now, and only run the source code that directly triggers the sample, saving the original input, actual output, and stopping point. Whether the input is preserved unchanged, changes locally, or produces an existing error, these three outcomes each point to different follow-up work. The advantage of this approach is that it does not turn unknown syntax boundaries into new commitments; the cost is that it cannot immediately change the result users see.

**Adjust local conditions.** Discuss a minimal change only after the sample has actually passed through a transformation check. The review needs to consider the structure that triggers the check alongside neighboring structures that should not trigger it. If a check such as `is_simple_lookup` serves only simple structures, the meaning of "simple" must not be expanded just because a complex combination looks similar. A candidate change must also explain why it will not subject neighboring expressions to the same rewrite. No frozen diff or test results are currently available, so only the selection criteria are retained here, without writing the outcome in advance.

**Stop explicitly.** If the existing node shapes cannot safely pass through the transformation, preserving an identifiable stopping point may be safer than forcing acceptance. Here, "stopping" must first be distinguished by layer: a sample not being accepted at the parser stage and a sample being terminated by `CannotTransform` after entering the transformation layer are not the same thing. The latter also does not automatically establish the user-facing error text or how the error propagates, because that information is not in the current material.

## How a Review Determines the Approach

The review material should start with a piece of source code that actually triggers this combination. When saving the original input and tool output, do not record only the last line; also record whether the output changes the structures on either side of await, whether there is any inconsistency between before and after transformation, and at what layer execution stops. If the output does not change, that must not be interpreted directly as "supported"; first confirm whether the sample passed through the expected entry point.

The second step is only to take local path notes. Along `src/black/trans.py`, record whether the sample encounters `hug_power_op`, `is_simple_lookup`, `is_simple_operand`, `handle_is_simple_look_up_prev`, or `handle_is_simple_lookup_forward`. For functions it encounters, record their direct neighbors and check results; do not force explanations for functions it does not encounter just for completeness. If the path exits elsewhere, preserve that exit point, and do not expand the proposal into a project-wide syntax walkthrough.

Only in the third step should a candidate diff be produced. The diff should answer two small questions: whether the sample's structure remains recognizable before and after the change, and whether expressions next to the sample are affected by the same change. If the current code snippet cannot answer these two questions, defer local condition adjustments. Failure at this point calls not for "adding a broader condition," but for acknowledging that the evidence has not yet reached a layer where changes can be made.

This also addresses counterexamples to the early hypothesis. A helper may check only leaves, lookup direction, or simple operands, without being responsible for the full acceptance process for `await ellipsis grammar`. Even if the names offer hints of proximity to `await`, `grammar`, or `expression`, that does not establish that the helper is the interface owner. Once an actual path is available, withdraw the original local-fix hypothesis if it bypasses these helpers; if it does enter a particular check, possible changes can only be discussed within the input shapes of that check.

## Review Trade-offs

On the interface side, the concern is more about whether boundaries can be explained than whether internal functions are exposed as guarantees. If local condition adjustments are ultimately adopted, the public record should describe the structures that do and do not trigger the check, without turning internal helpers in `trans.py` into a contract for callers. If explicit stopping is adopted, preserve the layer where execution stops and a reproducible input shape; do not describe "not formatted" indiscriminately as parser rejection.

On the implementation side, the risk is conflating syntax problems with transformation problems. If the sample has not yet entered this file, continuing to modify `TErr` or lookup helpers will only compound the misattribution; if the sample has already been rewritten by a condition, describing the result as "completely unprocessed" is also inaccurate. Keeping the existing path is therefore not an empty option: it first pins down the control flow, output, and stopping point, leaving original records that can be compared for later decisions.

For now, the discussion of migration costs can go no further than outlining their boundaries. The existing material contains no caller results, version matrix, or compatibility samples, so it cannot support declaring a Python version range or quantifying how many expressions local condition adjustments would affect. If a change is eventually considered, the costs include, at a minimum, regression checks for neighboring structures, checking whether previous output changes, and checking whether the existing stopping behavior is retained when this combination is not accepted; these are questions for the review to ask, not results already obtained.

## Withdrawal Conditions

Withdraw the proposal to "make a local fix within `trans.py`" if any of the following occurs: the triggering sample does not reach that file; the sample reaches it but does not pass through the check under discussion; or the candidate diff cannot explain why it leaves neighboring expressions unchanged. Withdrawal restores the existing path and stopping behavior, rather than merging speculative conditions into the code.

Still unresolved are the sample's exact control flow, whether the current output meets expectations, and whether responsibility ultimately lies with the parser, node organization, or transformation conditions. Once these questions are supported by direct input and output, consolidate the three approaches into a single decision. The current proposal stops here, without presenting unfinished verification as a conclusion about the interface.

```python

```

First preserve the original f-string; do not manually delete expressions, replace quotes, or rewrap the output beforehand. Once the input has been modified, subsequent comparisons can only establish behavior for the modified sample.

## First distinguish the symptoms

```text
Is there a reproducible input/output pair?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only the description "f-string expression line splitting"
│  │  └─ Stop: provide the original input and the result the user saw
│  └─ Only a screenshot or a one-line diff

```

"Format again" is only intended to check whether the behavior is stable, not to treat the second output as the original evidence. If the two results differ, first record the difference and stop; do not attribute unstable results to linegen.

## Structural branch

First examine the boundaries on both sides of the expression. Record the following: the plain text in f-string, where the expression starts and ends, whether any adjacent content follows the expression, and the line boundaries before and after formatting. In particular, preserve the content after the expression's closing brace; copying only the characters inside the braces may discard the adjacent text that actually triggers line splitting.

Trace the f-string token stream backward to see how the input enters parsing and subsequent objects, and record the first differing token or node. Without the location of that difference, do not infer the parsing cause from the final line layout.

Only if the token stream is the same and the output changes only during line generation should you continue to examine the adjacency path for `src/black/linegen.py`. At that point, compare:

- Whether the expression itself already occupies a whole line;
- Whether long content triggers a new line boundary only after the closing brace;
- Whether adjacent content is treated as the same output segment;
- Whether the content on the current `Line` is consistent with the newlines ultimately written.

The easiest approach is to shorten the expression, delete the plain text after the closing brace, or compare only the final diff. # Decision record: first newline style

The first notes on this were about the first newline in the formatted output. The input may already contain a mix of newline forms; earlier discussions tended to frame this as a whole-file newline policy, but we first need to look at the first visible newline and subsequent handling separately. That first newline is the point users are most likely to notice in the output, and it also affects whether later examples look like the same kind of result.

The provisional scope is the handoff between formatter input and output, without treating tokens, parse trees, or helper state themselves as part of the external contract. Test names and assertions should describe the form used in the input and what readers can see after formatting; don't assert directly on internal helper functions, local state, or an intermediate value just to lock in the current implementation.

There were two approaches at the time.

- Treat the first newline as an ordinary character, exactly like subsequent newlines, and have all examples check only the final text.
- Record the style of the first newline separately, then use that record during output to determine the opening portion of the formatted text.

We started with the second approach. Not because it necessarily explains every input, but because it gives the disagreement a concrete focus: where the first newline is read from, when it is overwritten, and what is retained when the input is mixed. The first approach would bury these questions in a comparison of the entire string, making it hard to tell on failure whether detection, formatting, or the example itself was off.

This decision also doesn't mean every kind of mixed input already has an answer. For CRLF, standalone CR, and text containing multiple forms, initial detection and subsequent formatting still need to be checked separately. Around fmt directives and comments in particular, visual inspection of the output is not enough; they may change the reading boundary, but should not simply be folded into the first-newline rule.

The earlier investigation pointed to `tests/test_black.py`. The initial draft treated it only as a starting point for revisiting the investigation: it is a suitable place for user-visible regression cases, which can be read alongside existing names such as `state`, `first`, `newline`, `style`, and `normalization`. Dependencies such as `asyncio`, `inspect`, `io`, and `logging` are visible at the top of the file, but this record does not use that to assign first-newline handling to any of them.

At this stage, we are not treating preview or enabled_features as switches for the first-newline rule. If they appear in an example, first explain which formatting path the example verifies, then decide whether to include them in the comparison. The target version should not be used as a reason to hide differences either; a syntax example requiring a target version does not mean that the target version determines how newline style is identified.

Still to fill in:

- How to preserve other forms after the first recognizable newline in mixed input as counterexamples;
- Whether boundaries around directives and immediately adjacent comments can make identification of the first newline unstable;
- Whether regression coverage needs to include both ordinary formatted text and input containing already formatted fragments.

The decision at this point only requires treating the first newline as an independently verifiable object and writing regressions against user-visible results. The other branches remain open pending actual verification.

# Decision Record for First-Line Newline Style

When this record was first written, the first line ending was merely a trouble spot in a regression test case: the same input looked no different in different people's editors, yet the first line ending after formatting was enough to make the entire output look different. Looking back, the problem was not about giving line endings a more complicated name, but about how we had conflated three layers: the characters actually present in the input text, the first style recorded during reading, and the formatted result ultimately delivered to the user.

The old record focused on the second layer. That was an appropriate place to stop at the time, because we first needed to avoid turning the discussion of line endings across an entire file into a vague problem with no starting point. Now that this review has been added, we still retain the record of that layer, but no longer let it carry the conclusion on its own. Tests and decisions should both focus on user-visible results; internal state can only help pinpoint issues and should not replace assertions about the results.

This is not a rewrite of the global line-ending strategy. We are closing out only first-newline-style normalization here: identifying the first newline style when reading formatting input, and making that identification verifiable through regression test cases. Related topics such as the module docstring, type-comment spacing, the f-string token stream, and backslash continuation newline forms may appear in the same file, but this decision must not be used to rewrite them all as the same rule. Each has its own syntactic position and failure modes.

## What the Initial Record Said

The initial draft offered a useful but incomplete judgment: do not treat the first newline as merely part of the ordinary text. If every case relies solely on comparing large blocks of final text, then when a test case fails, it is hard to tell whether detection of the first line ending was lost, the formatting stage did not use the detected value, or the test case itself specified the mixed input incorrectly. The record therefore retained `state`, `first`, `newline`, `style`, and `normalization` as lookup terms, to remind anyone investigating not to infer every internal step by working backward from the entire output.

This judgment has not been withdrawn. However, it was once interpreted too broadly, as though finding a state alone were enough to declare the formatting behavior stable. That is not enough. state is a local record made during reading, not an output contract; it only helps pinpoint issues when it appears alongside the input test case and the formatted result. To prevent later readers from treating the initial draft as an implementation guide, we explicitly retain a narrower use here: state is used to check whether the first newline was identified and passed along, while the user-visible result is used to determine whether the regression is confirmed.

The initial draft also listed CRLF, a standalone CR, and mixed input as items to verify. These terms did not automatically imply a priority rule. They only indicate that the input text may not follow a neat, single style, and that passing one ordinary LF example cannot be interpreted as covering all combinations. Future examples should state the input form near the example itself, rather than merely mentioning mixed cases in the explanation.

## Approaches compared at the time

The first approach was not to retain any information about the first occurrence. The reader would pass the various newline forms to subsequent generic processing, and tests would check only the final formatted text. Its advantage was apparent simplicity: no extra state and no first value to explain. The problem was that once the first-line result changed, a failure could only point to the entire string. The person investigating would have to go back and forth among the tokenizer, output concatenation, and test fixtures, unable to tell from the failure text whether the original style had already been discarded.

The second approach was to record the style at the first occurrence, but restrict its use to the current formatting run. It did not promise to preserve every kind of newline in the input verbatim, nor did it require all subsequent newlines to be copied one by one. It simply treated the first recognizable newline as an explicit observation point, allowing what was read and the beginning visible to the user to be discussed in the same regression test.

A third approach was proposed: infer a uniform style for the entire input from the style that appears first, then process all output according to that inference. This direction was not included in the decision at the time. The reason was not that uniform output is necessarily wrong, but that it extends an observation at the first occurrence into an intention for the whole file, and we had no evidence that this extension was appropriate for directives, comments, already formatted fragments, or mixed input. If a whole-file strategy is needed in the future, input classification, conflict handling, and migration scope should be proposed separately, not slipped in through first-newline-style normalization.

The fourth approach was to put the decision logic in the test helper layer, having tests first rewrite the input into the expected form and then invoke formatting. This direction was not adopted either. It would make the examples look stable, but obscure what the formatting process actually read. In particular, for failing examples, transformations performed beforehand by the fixture would break the traceable correspondence among input, detection, and result.

Therefore, the current decision continues with the second approach: the first newline style is information local to a single formatting run; regression tests check the user-visible formatted result; no whole-file rule is inferred from it, and fixture rewriting is not treated as a fix.

## Terminology and what it covers

The "first newline" refers to the position of the newline read first from the formatting input, not where the first line appears to break on screen, nor the position of the first newline in the formatted text. If the source text begins with a comment, blank line, string, or directive, readers can easily conflate the first visually apparent section with the read position; examples need to make this difference visible, rather than merely assuming in the description that they are the same.

"Style" refers only to the line-break form at that location. It is not Mode, nor Preview, and even less is it a shorthand for target_versions. Mode can change the formatting path, Preview can allow some layouts that are still experimental, and target_versions can restrict whether a given syntax can be parsed; these objects may all appear in the same test file, but they and the first-line line break belong to different dimensions. When a sample uses them all at once, it should state separately the condition each one serves.

"normalization" also needs to be narrowed here. It does not mean that every input is forced into some fixed text style, nor does it mean carrying every original character unchanged into the output. It refers to formatting around the first newline style being able to consistently produce the user-facing result, with that result verifiable through regression testing. If whether the input's other line breaks are preserved is still disputed, that uncertainty should remain in the sample or a subsequent record; do not use the word normalization to conceal it.

The "user-visible result" is the formatted text itself. It does not include helper function names, temporary variable names, or local state selected internally by the test. Assertions can be expressed through strings, file contents, or existing test entry points, but the reader should be able to tell from the assertion what the input is and why the result matters, without first having to understand some private helper process.

## Recheck location and local reading

The recheck entry point remains `tests/test_black.py`. Older investigation records point from the issue name and call name to this file, and the current review has not redirected it elsewhere. This file is a suitable place for the regression test because it is close to the comparison between user input and the formatted result; but it is not an implementation-ownership table. The file header shows `import asyncio`, `import inspect`, `import io`, and `import logging`; these dependencies indicate that the test file handles more than one kind of testing work, so the import list cannot be used to infer that first-line line-break handling necessarily belongs to a particular branch.

When reading this entry point, first look for the examples and assertions adjacent to `first`, `newline`, `style`, `detected`, `crlf`, `formatted`, `mixed`, and `input`. Then check whether `mode`, `enabled_features`, `preview`, or `uses` is involved in the example. This is not meant to prescribe a fixed order for reading the code, but to avoid mistaking a regression test intended only to pin down user-facing results for a complete explanation of Mode or Preview.

If `tokenize`, parse tree, Leaf, or Line appears in an example, do not immediately include them in this decision either. They may simply be other test subjects in the same file, or concepts adjacent to the boundary between reading and formatting. The record on the first newline only needs to confirm: whether the first form encountered in the input was detected, whether the formatting process used the relevant information, and whether the final text matches the example's expectations. Objects beyond these three points need their own supporting material.

Earlier records suggested initially grouping failures into three categories: detection, formatting, or examples. This classification can still be used for troubleshooting, but it must not be used to assign causes automatically. For example, a failure with mixed input may appear to be a mismatch in the final text, when the actual issue may be that the example does not make clear where the first occurrence is; conversely, an apparently correct state does not prove that the string assertion targets the right location. Every review must examine the original input and the formatted result together.

## Counterexamples are not add-ons

A regression test with ordinary input is the easiest kind to write: the text starts with a single newline form, and formatting also produces a stable result. This is valuable, but it only proves that this one input path has not regressed. The decision about the first newline's style needs to be documented separately because ordinary input makes "the first occurrence was detected" and "the entire input was already consistent" look like the same fact.

Mixed input should be retained as a counterexample in its own right. The point here is not to assume an answer for every mixed combination, but to make the example explicit about which form appears first, which form appears later, and which part of the formatted result the assertion targets. Otherwise, someone who later sees `mixed` will only know that the input is inconsistent, without knowing why the first newline style matters in that example.

The CRLF example should not be treated as merely a renamed version of an ordinary LF example either. It needs to preserve the actual input form so readers can tell whether detection of the first occurrence covers that form. If the test framework or text construction process has already normalized the input before calling the formatter, the example loses this observational value; this is precisely why the approach of rewriting fixtures in advance was not adopted.

The case of a standalone CR must likewise not be grouped with CRLF simply because it is rare. Their textual representations differ, and regression test authors should at least be clear about which one they are writing. This record does not prescribe an assumed output rule for it; without explicit examples and results, calling both "Windows line endings" and sharing assertions will only conceal an unconfirmed branch.

Empty input and input without any line breaks are another class of edge cases. They provide no first line break, so state cannot be expected to produce a style as it does for input with line breaks. What should be checked here is whether formatting can still handle them normally, rather than artificially creating a value for a first occurrence that does not exist. This also avoids misrepresenting "not detected" as proof of some default style.

Input that starts with comments needs separate attention. Line breaks before and after comments can make the visual order and reading order unintuitive, especially when the object being formatted immediately follows a comment. The first-line rule should not be considered correct merely because the output looks good; examples should retain the beginning of the input so reviewers can determine whether the first line break is before the comment, after it, or inside the object being formatted.

fmt directives remain an area that has not been fully settled. They may exclude a section of text from normal formatting, but that does not mean first-line detection can skip or arbitrarily override observations of the entire input. The earlier draft listed them as a risk, and later notes again pointed out that this area still contains unconfirmed details, so this record does not claim that all cases before and after a directive have been resolved.

Already formatted fragments should not automatically be treated as irrelevant input either. If a fragment remains unchanged because of a directive or for some other reason, the relationship between the first line break around it and the rest of the file may still affect the result users see. The current decision only requires tests to clearly document such fragments as adjacent conditions when necessary; it does not require a new set of rules for each type of directive.

## Retaining and Revising the Earlier Approach

The following passage retains the working assumption from the initial draft to help explain why it was not carried forward.

> Working assumption: As long as the first line break is recorded, subsequent differences in output style can be attributed to that record; the rest of the mixed input is not important for now.

This passage no longer applies. It equated "can be located" with "can be attributed." The record of the first occurrence is, of course, still an important observation point, but the later content of mixed input may affect whether the test text expresses the case clearly, and differences in the final string may also originate elsewhere. The revised statement is: recording the first occurrence makes the problem locatable; attribution still requires checking the input, relevant conditions, and formatting result together.

Another simplification that was discussed was that, as long as the output is uniform, the form of the first occurrence in the original input no longer needs to be retained in the test. This simplification was not adopted either. Whether uniform output is reasonable is a separate decision, and the current regression tests must at least retain enough text to identify the input form; otherwise, the tests might continue to pass even if the detection logic regresses.

Another misreading comes from preview. Some people may take examples with preview enabled as evidence that the first-line rule holds only under Preview. This interpretation has not been accepted. When Preview is an environmental condition for an example, it should be retained alongside that example; however, no material indicates that it is the switch controlling first-line style detection. Tying the two concepts inseparably together could lead to this regression test being mistakenly deleted when preview is later disabled or adjusted.

Similarly, enabled_features must not be written as the master switch for the first-line policy. If it appears in tests, it should be interpreted as a condition on a particular formatting path, rather than inferring from its name that it governs newline logic. This decision does not change the responsibility of enabled_features, nor does it introduce a feature flag intended solely for newlines.

## Current decision

The current decision can be implemented in four points.

First, the style of the first newline must be treated as an independent observed value in the input being formatted in this run. It is not an alias for the style of the entire file, nor an instruction for every newline in the output text.

Second, regression assertions must be based on the user-visible formatting result. Tests may inspect state or the detection process for diagnostic purposes, but they must not assert only internal names, helper-function calls, or intermediate state and then conclude that external behavior is protected.

Third, samples should retain the input form at the first occurrence. Ordinary input, CRLF, standalone CR, mixed input, an opening with comments, and nearby text that may be affected by fmt directives are different conditions for interpreting the input. They do not have to be combined in the same test, and should not share strings with no explanatory value merely because their names are similar.

Fourth, the current decision does not extend to a whole-file newline policy. If it later becomes necessary to define output precedence for all newlines, the complete behavior of mixed input, or bind this rule to a Mode, Preview, or target_versions, a clear plan and examples should be recorded separately. Those conclusions cannot be drawn directly from the first-occurrence handling here.

These four points preserve the intent of the initial draft: when something fails, there is still a specific observation point to inspect; at the same time, they correct the initial draft's boundary: an observation point cannot replace the user-visible result, nor a concrete explanation of mixed input.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> input
    state "Read formatted input" as input
    state "Detect first newline" as detect
    state "Record style at first occurrence" as first_style
    state "Format text" as format
    state "Compare user result" as assertion
    input --> detect
    detect --> first_style: First newline found
    detect --> format: No newline
    first_style --> format
    format --> assertion
    assertion --> [*]
```

The "no newline" label in the diagram does not mean that a particular style is the default, but that there is no first occurrence to identify. The diagram also does not show branches for every kind of CRLF, CR, or mixed input, because those are differences that the input examples should preserve, not a complete state table that has already been finalized.

## Relationship to Test Cases

BLK-216 are referenced only as entry points for regression testing. The work item in the card calls for adding a repository regression test for first-newline-style normalization, with assertions about user-visible results rather than internal helper function names. This requirement aligns with the second item in this record, so this decision treats it as the implementation direction, without expanding the card into a broader formatting plan.

Before writing the regression test, first determine whether the example actually provides a first newline. If the input contains no newline, the test can still be valuable, but it verifies handling in the absence of a first-occurrence style and should not pretend to cover the first-line rule. If the input contains a newline, the example should let readers see which form occurs first, rather than sending the text to the formatter only after it has been rewritten by a helper layer.

Assertions should focus on the formatted result. An assertion can be an explicit text comparison, or it can use the result entry point already present in the test file; the key is that the failure output should let someone determine the difference between the input and the result. If an assertion only says that some helper was called or some state is not empty, future changes may still preserve the internal path while changing the newlines users see.

Do not make a single regression test cover every syntax scenario. For example, examples with type parameters, await ellipsis grammar, or nested generic-bound tuples will obscure the newlines under test if they are only there to trigger an unrelated parsing path. These syntax constructs should only be included in the example when they are genuinely necessary for reading the first occurrence or producing the final text, with a note alongside explaining why they are there.

Layout topics such as long comprehension iterable wrapping, preview long dictionary values, and walrus grouping in with statements should be handled with the same restraint. They may appear nearby in `tests/test_black.py`, but they cannot provide substitute evidence for the first-line newline rule. A good regression test keeps the input conditions minimal while still showing the result protected by this decision.

excluded stdin passthrough is another boundary that must not be mixed in. If the stdin handling path has its own passthrough conditions, it cannot automatically be included in this decision just because newlines may also occur in it. When stdin needs to be tested, first explain how it relates to ordinary formatting input; without that information, the conclusions from ordinary file examples should not be extended to it.

per-invocation no-cache CLI mode, cache, and asynchronous blackd client are likewise not central to the current decision. They may affect how calls are made or how results are obtained, but there is no reason to treat them as controlling factors for first-position style merely because of adjacent terminology. If a failure later occurs only along these paths, record the calling environment and actual text separately; do not go back and turn this page into a general description of commands or services.

## Correction After a Review

After BLK-216 were linked and sent for processing, the review found that the old draft had not made the open question around directives and comments clear enough. The exact wording of the public addendum was: `One correction: in the Formatting directives and comments section, first-newline-style normalization still has one unconfirmed point.`

This sentence only says that this local point remains unconfirmed; it cannot be generalized into a complete design conclusion. Nor can it be used to negate the scope already established: regression tests should still assert user-visible results, and the first position remains an independent observation point. What needs to be corrected is the tone of the old draft. The old draft put directives and comments in the to-do list at the end, which could lead people to think that once ordinary examples passed, this section would automatically hold; it is now explicitly retained as an unconfirmed branch.

For comments, the next check should examine the comment's position relative to the first newline, rather than broadly comparing two categories of files, "with comments" and "without comments." Comments may appear at the beginning of the input or near the content to be formatted; whether different positions bear on the first-position observation is a separate question. The current material provides no result covering all comment positions, so a unified conclusion should not be invented.

For fmt directives, the next check must retain the text containing the directive and the newlines before and after it. The focus is not to treat the directive as an anomaly label, but to see whether it causes readers to misidentify the first position, whether it causes some part of the input to remain unchanged, and whether the final assertion still targets the user-visible result that this case is supposed to protect. If an example only has an ordinary newline after the directive, it cannot replace an example at the directive boundary.

This correction does not require immediately removing the old ordinary examples. Ordinary examples remain a stable baseline, but they can no longer be treated as a proxy under the directives/comments condition. Keeping the old examples allows later reviews to distinguish which new condition caused the problem, rather than flattening all historical results into an undifferentiated conclusion.

## Responsibility Boundaries

The responsibility boundary for this decision is narrow. The testing side is responsible for clearly documenting user-visible regressions and preserving the input form and output differences when a failure occurs. The formatting-logic side is responsible for ensuring that the first-position observation can affect the corresponding formatting process, rather than merely leaving behind a local record that no one uses. During review, determine whether the example truly demonstrates the externally visible result, rather than merely checking whether its name contains first or newline.

When a failure occurs only with mixed input, do not immediately classify it as "a complete failure of the newline rules". First check whether the example clearly specifies the location of the first occurrence, whether the input has already been rewritten before formatting, and whether the assertion compares the expected output range. If all of these are clear, then check whether information is lost between detection and formatting. This sequence avoids escalating a problem with how an example is expressed directly into a change in implementation scope.

When a failure occurs only next to comments or fmt directives, just record that adjacency. Do not turn it into a generalization about all comments, all directives, or all regions excluded from formatting. The current public addendum provides only one unconfirmed hint; turning it into a complete compatibility matrix would go beyond the material available this time.

When a failure occurs only under Mode, Preview, or target_versions conditions, each condition should likewise be retained separately. The condition may merely cause a particular piece of text to take a different formatting path, or it may indeed be related to first-occurrence handling. Without an actual comparison, the condition should not be removed, nor can it simply be claimed that the first-line rule is controlled by a particular switch.

## Notes on Retained Earlier Examples

### Earlier Example A: A Single Input Form

Early regression tests tended to start with a single newline form. This is still suitable as a minimal example: the input is clear, the formatted result is easy to read, and mixed text does not obscure failures. But it only demonstrates the result for that input form. If someone later treats it as a substitute for CRLF or mixed input, they should return to the counterexamples section of this record and add further examples, rather than broaden the interpretation of the old assertion.

### Earlier Example B: Checking Only Internal Records

There was once a suggestion to pin down the detected value first, then add string comparisons once the output examples had stabilized. This suggestion was not retained as the final form. It can serve as a temporary diagnostic approach, especially when checking whether the first occurrence is read; but as a long-term regression test, it shifts the maintenance focus from user-visible results to implementation details. This approach should now be treated as diagnostic material, rather than a completion criterion.

### Earlier Example C: Extending the Style at the First Occurrence to the Entire Text

This was also an extension of an early working assumption, which has since been overturned. The style at the first occurrence can be one input that determines formatting behavior, but it does not automatically mean that the entire file expresses the same stylistic intent. With mixed input in particular, the first occurrence may differ from the content that follows. This passage is retained so that future changes do not once again expand a local observation into a file-wide commitment.

## Areas Still Undecided

There is currently no output table covering all permutations of mixed input. Creating one would first require confirming which permutations reflect actual problems in user input, and which are merely differences caused by how fixtures are constructed. Directly listing a seemingly complete table would instead present results that have not been rechecked as established behavior.

The precedence between comments and fmt directives at all positions has not been decided either. What is known is that some points in this area remain unconfirmed; what is unknown is whether those points concern first-occurrence recognition, text preservation, or the final formatting layout. Subsequent examples should first pin down one of these positions, then determine which layer needs to change.

No decision has been made to extend the first-line newline rule to blackd, stdin, or asynchronous clients. These are different entry points. If external calls report differences on these paths, preserve the actual input and returned text before deciding whether the conclusions from the ordinary formatting regression here also apply.

No decision has been made to label this handling as Preview-only or non-Preview-only. If existing examples require Preview, that condition should be faithfully retained; but the condition's name alone is not enough to establish causation. If a feature flag is later confirmed to change how the first occurrence is handled, the specific input and result should be included in that change record.

## Where to stop during review

For this decision, review can stop when the following conditions are met: there is a regression test that preserves the input form at the first occurrence; the regression test checks the formatted result seen by the user; the ordinary path and the edge cases requiring special explanation have not been lumped into one broad assertion; the unconfirmed aspects of comments and fmt directives remain explicitly noted. Once these conditions are met, there is no need to list every newline, every syntax form, or every entry point just to make the page look more complete.

If a new failure appears, first classify it under the existing local conditions: no newline, a single form, CRLF, standalone CR, mixed input, adjacent to a comment, adjacent to a directive, or a specific Mode/Preview/target_versions condition. This classification only helps preserve the observed state; it does not replace judgment about the fix. If it does not fit any of these categories, record the actual input and result first as well, rather than insisting that it must be a first-line style issue.

Ultimately, the original draft's core trade-off still stands: the first newline needs a traceable local record; long-term regression tests must protect the formatted result users can see. Unlike the original draft, local records are no longer mistaken for complete causal attribution, and the fact that an ordinary sample passes is no longer extrapolated to the unconfirmed aspects of directives, comments, or mixed input.

# Release Automation Cache Tradeoff Record

This is an old tradeoff record. It records a limited choice made at the time in the black-release-automation queue, not an explanation of the later release process. Cache and the original setup are discussed together because, at the time, it was first necessary to preserve a revision that could still be reviewed; once the environment was rebuilt, the exit position, entry value, and cache conditions would all change, making the original failure difficult to compare with new results.

## Choice recorded at the time

The first option was to continue placing the state at `type parameters`. This avoided moving existing items, but `cache` would remain alongside the other conditions on the page; even if different outputs appeared later, it would be difficult to tell whether the difference came from the cache or the original setup.

The second option was to split out `cache` while retaining the current revision. This was not about establishing a new environment; it only made the cache an item that could be viewed independently while preserving the existing exit position. The record ultimately adopted the second option. The reason was narrow: it kept the observations from the same release queue in view and, at least, did not overwrite the original failure exit with the results of later cleanup.

No active callers of `Preview` were found at the time; withdrawing one item was recorded only as possibly requiring restoration of the old entry point. The original draft put these two gaps at the end and did not pursue them further, because that day's decision only chose between "what to preserve" and "what to rebuild first."

## Dissenting views left on record

Those opposed to the split worried that the sample was too narrow. That concern was not disproved: what was observed at the time was one original setup, not a set of interchangeable release results. Those in favor of preserving it believed that cleaning up the setup first and then adding a successful record would instead erase the conditions of the original exit.

Therefore, the old decision rested on a premise that now looks overly optimistic: as long as current revision remained, the exit and rollback assessment could later be completed from the same entry point. This premise was not validated at the time. It remains here to explain why, when the entry point, cache, and exit action later became inconsistent with one another, the earlier "split cache" cannot be taken to mean that the recovery problem had already been solved.

## Context added later

BLKA-003 originally required saving the exit code, black · Release Automation and the last segment of the logs before releasing the current revision. Later, this card was canceled because it duplicated the implementation card in the same document; the original card continued to be tracked. The canceled item was only the duplicate tracking location; this does not mean the save requirement itself had been completed.

The same card also contains a record from after an account or workspace switch: it stopped upon reaching the exit entry point. It did not show that the cache caused the halt, nor that the original setup was unusable; it only showed that treating "current revision is still there" as a sufficient condition in the old decision was unreliable. Once the account or workspace changed, the reachable entry point was already different, and the setup preserved earlier might not include the conditions needed for the subsequent exit.

The scope confirmation added afterward did not close out this issue either. It kept this record focused only on release automation's own revision, cache, entry point, and exit action, without using build results from elsewhere as a substitute for the assessment here.

## Exit and rollback recorded separately

BLKA-007 notes that black-release-aut is inconsistent with the rollback state of the exit action, and requires the rollback entry point and the exit action to be checked separately. This requirement goes directly to a blind spot in the old record: restoring the old entry point shows, at most, that the entry point was partially restored; it does not mean that the exit action also returned to its original state. The earlier wording did not make this distinction and should still be retained in the terms used at the time.

BLKA-008 also left an open item to investigate: at the end of the window, the current entry point was still set to the old value. The time at which the window ended must be preserved first, and then it must be determined whether this old value came from the old cache or the old task. In this record, the two sources cannot be treated as interchangeable: if the source is the old cache, only then is the cache-splitting choice directly relevant; if it is the old task, continuing to discuss cache will only misdirect the investigation.

The cold-start difference in BLKA-012 was also listed separately: the current entry point can be rerun after clearing its own cache; do not touch the shared cache yet. It was a probe added later, not a validation conclusion for the old decision. The old draft did not establish a way to handle the shared cache, so this addendum cannot be retroactively treated as an exit condition that had already been considered at the time.

BLKA-002 also retains the item to retrieve the original command parameters; it only entered the handling stage later. Missing parameters mean that, although the original setup was preserved, it may not be possible to rerun it as-is; this is why this page records only the tradeoff and does not describe it as reproducible release steps.

## Conclusions still retained

Retaining the current revision and separating `cache` from the way `type parameters` was placed was the decision made at the time, because the rebuilt environment should not overwrite the existing exit position. This conclusion is only useful for explaining why the environment was not immediately rebuilt that day.

The old entry value that appeared later, stopping at the exit entry point after switching accounts or workspaces, and the inconsistent rollback states were not accounted for by the original decision. They only expose the boundary of that old decision: cache, entry point, and exit action can no longer be treated as one thing. The original page is still at `docs/adj-black/decisions/black-release-automation-cache-vs-original-live-environment-tradeoffs.md`; related tracking can be accessed via BLKA-002, BLKA-003, BLKA-007, BLKA-008 and BLKA-012.

# Compatibility Directory Dual-State Incident Postmortem

This anomaly involved the same object in blib2to3 · Compatibility Catalog. The entry point reported different current revisions at two points in time, so the same compat object was recorded in two states. The issue was not merely a display difference: this directory covers the public contract, migration records, and caller compatibility. Anyone later relying on just one source would mix the old record with the current entry point.

The first discrepancy noticed was between the module docstring and the old record. The docstring was not immediately treated as the cause; it only showed that the available material had diverged. A rerun was then performed in another environment without changing the source code or commands, and the current revision was recorded. The rerun did not eliminate the divergence: the directory entry point still did not support the same assessment as the retained old record.

No further retries were made during incident handling. The original record was first exported as it stood at the time, and the recovery page was kept separately, so that a later refresh would not overwrite the fact that both states had been observed. The trade-off is that readers need to consult both documents, but this is more reliable than rewriting one as an annotation on the other. The current entry point for the incident export is:

`docs/adj-blib2to3/incidents/blib2to3-compatibility-catalog-same-object-with-two-states.md`

The recovery phase confirmed that Mode was recoverable. This result applies only to Mode; it does not explain the parse tree changes or prove that the two states came from the same path. The recovery page documents the recoverable behavior, while the original record preserves what was observed when the entry point was inconsistent. Neither should replace the other.

## Timeline

- On the first inspection of the directory, the module docstring differed from the old record. At that point, the only confirmed fact was that the materials for the same object did not agree; it was not possible to determine which should supersede the other.
- After a rerun under the original conditions in another environment, the current revision still differed from what had been seen at the entry point earlier. The source code and commands were not modified as a remediation step.
- The incident record was exported as it stood at the time, and further retries were stopped. Continuing to refresh the entry point might only yield a new final state, not recover the state first observed.

- When someone other than the author reviewed the incident, they could only confirm the existing divergence through the same entry point. Branches that had not been reproduced were left open for investigation; this was not used as a basis to extend the scope to neighboring projects.

During this period, the compatibility directory could not be treated as a single, time-independent source of state. Checks involving compat's public contract, migration records, or caller compatibility must identify both the record version and the current revision seen at the entry point. The available material supports only that "both states were available as evidence at the same time"; it does not support a claim that any caller had already experienced a specific outcome because of this discrepancy, nor can the mechanism behind the parse tree changes be inferred from the differing module docstring.

The directory object retains its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria; these were not moved to black-core as a result of this anomaly. The incident record captures only behavior observed on the directory side; neighboring services were not listed as causes or affected systems.

Why the parse tree changed remains unconfirmed. The existing record does not establish a causal link to Mode's recovery, nor does it contain enough process information to determine where each of the two current revisions originated. If this gap is filled later, new material should be added; the incident snapshot captured in this export should not be rewritten.

Another gap is the exact time of the first divergence. The available material establishes the sequence: first the docstring was found to differ from the old record, then the rerun in another environment was completed, and then the recovery results were retained. Exact times cannot be inferred from that sequence.

The original record, the recovery page, and the unresolved cause are retained so that future maintainers can distinguish "Mode has recovered" from "the parse tree changes remain unexplained." This page does not merge the two into a single conclusion.
